claim: Prokaryotic nanocompartments, also known as encapsulins, are a recently discovered proteinaceous organelle-like compartment in prokaryotes that compartmentalize cargo enzymes.
source: Prokaryotic nanocompartments, also known as encapsulins, are a recently discovered proteinaceous organelle-like compartment in prokaryotes that compartmentalize cargo enzymes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about encapsulins that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A novel encapsulin exists in the freshwater cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942.
source: Here, we describe a novel encapsulin in the freshwater cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including protein purification, microscopy, and structural analysis.

claim: The SrpI nanocompartment is upregulated upon sulfate starvation.
source: This nanocompartment is upregulated upon sulfate starvation and encapsulates a cysteine desulfurase enzyme via an N-terminal targeting sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from sulfate starvation experiments and mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The SrpI encapsulin encapsulates a cysteine desulfurase enzyme via an N-terminal targeting sequence.
source: This nanocompartment is upregulated upon sulfate starvation and encapsulates a cysteine desulfurase enzyme via an N-terminal targeting sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vivo and in vitro loading experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The structure of the SrpI nanocompartment complex has been determined to 2.2 Å resolution using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Using cryo-electron microscopy, we have determined the structure of the nanocompartment complex to 2.2 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and structural analysis presented in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: The activity of the cysteine desulfurase is enhanced upon encapsulation.
source: Lastly, biochemical characterization of the complex demonstrated that the activity of the cysteine desulfurase is enhanced upon encapsulation.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Subcellular compartmentalization is an essential strategy used by cells to facilitate metabolic pathways that are incompatible with the rest of the cytosol.
source: Subcellular compartmentalization is an essential strategy used by cells to facilitate metabolic pathways that are incompatible with the rest of the cytosol.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge and is referenced in the context of the introduction.

claim: Prokaryotes partition metabolic pathways into unique chemical environments using subcellular compartments.
source: Contrary to common misconceptions that organelles are exclusive to eukaryotes, even prokaryotes partition metabolic pathways into unique chemical environments using subcellular compartments (Grant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grant et al., 2018.

claim: Carboxysomes sequester the enzyme rubisco and facilitate substrate channeling by increasing the local concentration of CO2.
source: For example, studies of the bacterial microcompartments called carboxysomes have shown how the complex sequesters the enzyme rubisco and facilitates substrate channeling by increasing the local concentration of CO2 (Oltrogge et al., 2020; Mangan et al., 2016; Kerfeld et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oltrogge et al., 2020; Mangan et al., 2016; Kerfeld et al., 2018.

claim: The propane-diol utilization (PDU) microcompartment sequesters a cytotoxic aldehyde intermediate from the cytoplasm.
source: For example, the propane-diol utilization (PDU) microcompartment sequesters a cytotoxic aldehyde intermediate from the cytoplasm and allows it to be subsequently converted by downstream, compartmentalized enzymes to efficiently generate the end products of the pathway (Sampson and Bobik, 2008; Crowley et al., 2010; Chowdhury et al., 2015; Kerfeld et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sampson and Bobik, 2008; Crowley et al., 2010; Chowdhury et al., 2015; Kerfeld et al., 2018.

claim: Prokaryotic nanocompartments were discovered in 2008.
source: Recently, another class of protein-bounded compartments, known as prokaryotic nanocompartments, has been discovered (Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: Encapsulins are typically found as a two-gene system which encodes a shell protein that self-assembles into an icosahedral capsid-like compartment, and a cargo protein that becomes encapsulated by the shell through a targeting peptide sequence.
source: They are typically found as a two-gene system which encodes a shell protein that self-assembles into an icosahedral capsid-like compartment, and a cargo protein that becomes encapsulated by the shell through a targeting peptide sequence (Giessen, 2016; Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giessen, 2016; Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: Many functionally diverse cargo proteins have been found to be associated with encapsulins, including ferritin-like proteins (FLP), iron mineralizing encapsulin cargo from firmicutes (IMEF), DyP-type peroxidases, and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase (HAO).
source: Many functionally diverse cargo proteins have been found to be associated with encapsulins, including ferritin-like proteins (FLP), iron mineralizing encapsulin cargo from firmicutes (IMEF), DyP-type peroxidases, and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase (HAO) (Sutter et al., 2008; Giessen et al., 2019; Giessen and Silver, 2017; Xing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sutter et al., 2008; Giessen et al., 2019; Giessen and Silver, 2017; Xing et al., 2020.

claim: DyP-containing encapsulins from Myxococcus xanthus have been implicated in nutrient starvation and oxidative stress responses.
source: Notably, the DyP-containing encapsulins from Myxococcus xanthus have been implicated in nutrient starvation and oxidative stress responses (Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2019; McHugh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2019; McHugh et al., 2014.

claim: FLP and IMEF containing encapsulins appear to be involved in iron storage and mitigation of toxic reactive oxygen species products of the Fenton reaction due to free iron during oxidative stress.
source: The FLP and IMEF containing encapsulins appear to be involved in iron storage and mitigation of toxic reactive oxygen species products of the Fenton reaction due to free iron during oxidative stress (Giessen et al., 2019; Giessen and Silver, 2017; He et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giessen et al., 2019; Giessen and Silver, 2017; He et al., 2016.

claim: The HAO cargo in anammox bacteria has been hypothesized to reduce a cytotoxic hydroxylamine metabolic intermediate.
source: Encapsulins are also thought to be integral to highly specialized metabolism, such as that found in anammox bacteria, in which the HAO cargo has been hypothesized to reduce a cytotoxic hydroxylamine metabolic intermediate (Giessen and Silver, 2017; Kartal et al., 2013; Xing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giessen and Silver, 2017; Kartal et al., 2013; Xing et al., 2020.

claim: Encapsulation of redox reactions is a recurring theme among encapsulins.
source: Despite this diversity, encapsulation of redox reactions is a recurring theme (Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: A unifying feature of the encapsulin nanocompartments is the shared HK97 phage-like fold of the shell protein.
source: A unifying feature of the encapsulin nanocompartments is the shared HK97 phage-like fold of the shell protein (Giessen and Silver, 2017; Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giessen and Silver, 2017; Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: Bacteriophages belonging to the order Caudovirales possess a major capsid protein that is structurally homologous to the HK97 fold.
source: Bacteriophages belonging to the order Caudovirales also possess a major capsid protein that is structurally homologous to the HK97 fold.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about bacteriophage structure.

claim: An evolutionary relationship between encapsulins and Caudovirales capsid proteins has been proposed.
source: Given the shared homology of encapsulins and Caudovirales capsid proteins, an evolutionary relationship between the two has been proposed (Koonin and Krupovic, 2018; Krupovic et al., 2019; Krupovic and Koonin, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koonin and Krupovic, 2018; Krupovic et al., 2019; Krupovic and Koonin, 2017.

claim: Family 1 encapsulins comprise a minor fraction of all encapsulin systems.
source: This search suggested that previously published encapsulins, hereafter referred to as Family 1 encapsulins, comprise a minor fraction of all encapsulin systems.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis referenced in the text and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Family 2 encapsulins are more prevalent than Family 1 encapsulins.
source: This novel family is even more prevalent than Family 1 encapsulins (Supplementary file 1) and is present in many model organisms.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Family 2 encapsulins are distinct from the previously published Family 1 systems.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the encapsulin shell proteins revealed that Family 2 encapsulins are distinct from the previously published Family 1 systems (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Family 2 divides into two distinct subfamilies, Family 2a and Family 2b.
source: Family 2 further divides into what we propose as two distinct subfamilies, Family 2a and Family 2b.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic clustering shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Family 2a is found adjacent to sulfur metabolism genes whereas Family 2b neighbors genes involved in terpenoid synthesis.
source: Notably, the two subfamilies are found in distinct genomic contexts. Family 2a is found adjacent to sulfur metabolism genes whereas Family 2b neighbors genes involved in terpenoid synthesis (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genomic neighborhood analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A cysteine desulfurase gene is most prevalent among genes neighboring the Family 2a subfamily.
source: Most prevalent among the Family 2a subfamily was the co-occurrence of a neighboring cysteine desulfurase gene, while the Family 2b shell genes were found to most often neighbor a polyprenyl diphosphate synthase gene (Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by genomic neighborhood data in Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claim: Family 2b shell genes most often neighbor a polyprenyl diphosphate synthase gene.
source: Most prevalent among the Family 2a subfamily was the co-occurrence of a neighboring cysteine desulfurase gene, while the Family 2b shell genes were found to most often neighbor a polyprenyl diphosphate synthase gene (Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by genomic neighborhood data in Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claim: The CRP/FNR cyclic nucleotide-binding domain is predominantly found in the Family 2b shell sequences but not Family 2a.
source: The individual subfamilies can also be defined by the CRP/FNR cyclic nucleotide-binding domain that is predominantly found in the Family 2b shell sequences but not Family 2a.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of the two subfamilies.

claim: Family 2a encapsulins are widespread and found distributed in a polyphyletic fashion throughout 13 bacterial phyla.
source: Our focus for the remainder of the paper will be on the Family 2a subfamily, which is widespread and found distributed in a polyphyletic fashion throughout 13 bacterial phyla (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The SrpI shell protein eluted with an estimated molecular weight of approximately 2 MDa.
source: Expression of the shell gene in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells, followed by purification and size-exclusion chromatography, revealed that the protein eluted with an estimated molecular weight of ≈2 MDa (Figure 1C), the typical size for many previously characterized encapsulins (Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Snijder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Snijder et al., 2016.

claim: The SrpI complex forms a nanocompartment with an average diameter of 25 ± 1 nm.
source: Negative stain transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of the purified sample indicated the complex forms a nanocompartment with an average diameter of 25 ± 1 nm (n = 180) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by negative stain TEM data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The encapsulin shell gene (Synpcc7942_B2662) is upregulated upon sulfur starvation in S. elongatus.
source: Previous work by Nicholson and colleagues in S. elongatus demonstrated that the encapsulin shell gene (Synpcc7942_B2662) is one of many whose mRNA expression level is upregulated upon sulfur starvation (Nicholson et al., 1995; Nicholson and Laudenbach, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nicholson et al., 1995; Nicholson and Laudenbach, 1995.

claim: The SrpI gene is found on a plasmid encoding many sulfur-related genes.
source: Thus, this gene, which is found on a plasmid encoding many sulfur-related genes, was termed SrpI for Sulfur regulated plasmid-encoded gene-I (Chen et al., 2008; Nicholson and Laudenbach, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008; Nicholson and Laudenbach, 1995.

claim: Sulfur starvation in cyanobacteria results in a chlorosis phenotype due to the degradation of phycobilisomes.
source: Consistent with previous studies of sulfur starvation in cyanobacteria, we observed the expected chlorosis phenotype due to the degradation of phycobilisomes (Collier and Grossman, 1992; Cameron and Pakrasi, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collier and Grossman, 1992; Cameron and Pakrasi, 2010.

claim: Chlorosis was confirmed by loss of phycocyanin absorbance at 620 nm.
source: Chlorosis was confirmed by loss of phycocyanin absorbance at 620 nm (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by absorbance spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 48 hr of sulfur starvation, the top hits by total spectral counts were the putative encapsulin shell protein, SrpI, and the product of the neighboring gene (Synpcc7942_B2661), a cysteine desulfurase.
source: After 48 hr of sulfur starvation, the top hits, as determined by total spectral counts, were the putative encapsulin shell protein, SrpI, and the product of the neighboring gene (Synpcc7942_B2661), a cysteine desulfurase (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Knockout mutants for SrpI and cysteine desulfurase in S. elongatus PCC 7942 did not yield a growth defect phenotype under nutrient replete nor sulfur starvation conditions.
source: While we were able to detect upregulation of SrpI and cysteine desulfurase during sulfur starvation, knockout mutants for these genes in S. elongatus PCC 7942 did not yield a growth defect phenotype under nutrient replete nor sulfur starvation conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SrpI-associated cysteine desulfurase (CyD) possesses a unique N-terminal domain in addition to the canonical cysteine desulfurase domain.
source: Sequence alignment of the five cysteine desulfurases found in the S. elongatus genome revealed that the SrpI-associated cysteine desulfurase (Synpcc7942_B2661), hereafter named CyD, possesses a unique N-terminal domain in addition to the canonical cysteine desulfurase domain (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CyD is shared by cysteine desulfurases found adjacent to SrpI homologs in species possessing this encapsulin system.
source: This N-terminal domain is shared by cysteine desulfurases found adjacent to SrpI homologs in species possessing this encapsulin system.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis of homologous systems.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CyD is highly disordered.
source: Structural prediction using the primary sequence of the SrpI-associated CyD revealed that the N-terminal domain (NTD) is highly disordered (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by disorder prediction analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Intrinsically disordered domains evolve rapidly, preserving bulk chemical characteristics even as the sequence diverges greatly.
source: Intrinsically disordered domains are known to evolve rapidly, preserving bulk chemical characteristics even as the sequence diverges greatly (Moesa et al., 2012; Varadi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moesa et al., 2012; Varadi et al., 2015.

claim: Two motifs, 'LARLANEFFS' and 'AASPYYFLDG', can be found in most SrpI-associated CyD sequences.
source: However, two motifs, 'LARLANEFFS' and 'AASPYYFLDG', can be found in most SrpI-associated CyD sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence motif analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: The entire 225 amino acid N-terminal domain from CyD fused to sfGFP (CyD 1–225-sfGFP) yielded the highest loading signal.
source: The entire 225 amino acid N-terminal domain from CyD fused to sfGFP (CyD 1–225-sfGFP) yielded the highest loading signal.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE and fluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Targeting with the first 100 amino acids of the NTD functioned, albeit not as efficiently as the full N-terminus.
source: Targeting with the first 100 amino acids of the NTD also functioned, albeit not as efficiently as the full N-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE and fluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The entire cysteine desulfurase fused to sfGFP was encapsulated, yet not as well as the 225-NTD.
source: The entire cysteine desulfurase fused to sfGFP was also encapsulated, yet again not as well as the 225-NTD.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE and fluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CyD 155–183-sfGFP, containing the conserved motif of 'AASPYYFLDG', was not sufficient to sequester cargo within the compartment.
source: Lastly, CyD 155–183-sfGFP, containing the conserved motif of 'AASPYYFLDG', was not sufficient to sequester cargo within the compartment, nor was the non-tagged sfGFP construct.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE and fluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only the 225NTD-sfGFP construct displayed GFP fluorescence in the high-molecular-weight band, indicative of sfGFP loading.
source: Only the 225NTD-sfGFP construct displayed GFP fluorescence in the high-molecular-weight band, indicative of sfGFP loading (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro loading assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The native cysteine desulfurase cargo was encapsulated in vitro.
source: We were also able to load the full-length cysteine desulfurase in vitro using the same procedure. We observed encapsulation of the native cargo as indicated by the co-elution of cargo in the compartment fraction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro loading assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The disordered NTD is essential for cargo loading.
source: Lastly, we found that the disordered NTD is essential for cargo loading. A mutant CyD lacking the entire N-terminal domain (ΔNTD-CyD) was not measurably encapsulated, as evidenced by separate elution of compartment and truncated cargo (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro loading assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A clear difference in density on the shell interior was observed when comparing the apo-SrpI encapsulin (no cargo) to the holo-SrpI encapsulin (CyD loaded).
source: Even in raw micrographs, a clear difference in density on the shell interior was observed when comparing the apo-SrpI encapsulin (no cargo) to the holo-SrpI encapsulin (CyD loaded) (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is supported by negative stain TEM data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: The apo-SrpI capsid is permissive to uranyl formate stain.
source: The lack of density within the interior of the apo-SrpI capsid also demonstrates that the shell is permissive to uranyl formate stain, which would also allow definition of internal features for the cargo-loaded sample.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative stain TEM reconstruction shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Clear density for the CyD exists at one of the sites of threefold symmetry within the complex.
source: For the cargo-loaded structure, clear density for the CyD exists at one of the sites of threefold symmetry within the complex (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by negative stain TEM reconstruction shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A difference map revealed density corresponding to 1–2 copies of the cysteine desulfurase.
source: A difference map, created by subtracting apo-SrpI from the holo-SrpI structure, revealed density corresponding to 1–2 copies of the cysteine desulfurase (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by difference map analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: All encapsulin structures published thus far have belonged to the Family 1 encapsulins.
source: All encapsulin structures published thus far have belonged to the Family 1 encapsulins.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of the published literature on encapsulin structures.

claim: Family 1 encapsulin structures are all icosahedral, vary in size from 24 to 42 nm in diameter, and have a triangulation number of T = 1, T = 3, or T = 4.
source: These structures are all icosahedral, vary in size from 24 to 42 nm in diameter, and have a triangulation number of T = 1, T = 3, or more recently, T = 4 (Sutter et al., 2008; Akita et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2014; Giessen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sutter et al., 2008; Akita et al., 2007; McHugh et al., 2014; Giessen et al., 2019.

claim: The SrpI encapsulin structure was resolved at 2.2 Å resolution.
source: Cryo-EM analysis was performed on purified holo-SrpI to resolve the shell structure at 2.2 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: The SrpI encapsulin structure represents the first Family 2 encapsulin structure and is the highest resolution structure for an encapsulin to date.
source: This represents the first Family 2 encapsulin structure and is the highest resolution structure for an encapsulin to date, allowing for accurate atomic model building (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claim: The SrpI encapsulin is 24.5 nm in diameter and has a T = 1 icosahedral capsid formed by the self-assembly of 60 SrpI monomeric subunits.
source: The SrpI encapsulin is 24.5 nm in diameter and has a T = 1 icosahedral capsid formed by the self-assembly of 60 SrpI monomeric subunits (Figure 6A), similar to previously reported encapsulin structures.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The SrpI monomer shares the canonical HK97 fold found in Family 1 encapsulins and Caudovirales bacteriophages.
source: Given the structural similarity of the entire shell, it is unsurprising that the SrpI monomer also shares the canonical HK97 fold found in Family 1 encapsulins and Caudovirales bacteriophages (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The Family 2a SrpI possesses an extended N-terminal arm (N-arm) that is more characteristic of bacteriophage structures.
source: However, unlike other Family 1 encapsulin shell proteins, the Family 2a SrpI possesses an extended N-terminal arm (N-arm) that is more characteristic of bacteriophage structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C; Duda and Teschke, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C and citation to Duda and Teschke, 2019.

claim: The N-arm of the SrpI shell intertwines with the neighboring subunit to create a chainmail-like topology.
source: Similar to other HK97 bacteriophage capsids, the N-arm of the SrpI shell intertwines with the neighboring subunit to create a chainmail-like topology (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The vertices of the SrpI encapsulin protrude from the capsid yielding a raised 'spike' morphology not found in the Family 1 encapsulins.
source: The vertices of the SrpI encapsulin protrude from the capsid yielding a raised 'spike' morphology not found in the Family 1 encapsulins (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The A-domain of SrpI that forms a pore at the fivefold axis is composed of residues that are positively charged.
source: Interestingly, the A-domain of SrpI that forms a pore at the fivefold axis is composed of residues that are positively charged (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 5), in contrast to the negatively charged fivefold axis pore of Family 1 encapsulins (Giessen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by electrostatic analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 5, and citation to Giessen et al., 2019.

claim: The fivefold pore at the capsid vertices creates a selective barrier to allow encapsulin substrates into the compartment lumen.
source: It is thought that the fivefold pore at the capsid vertices creates a selective barrier to allow encapsulin substrates into the compartment lumen (Giessen et al., 2019; Nichols et al., 2017; Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giessen et al., 2019; Nichols et al., 2017; Sutter et al., 2008.

claim: At physiological pH for S. elongatus growing in light (pH 8–8.4), roughly 30–54% of free cysteine will have a net charge of −1.
source: At physiological pH for S. elongatus growing in light, pH 8–8.4 (Mangan et al., 2016), roughly 30–54% of free cysteine will have a net charge of −1 and therefore could traverse the positively charged pore exterior (Cameselle et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mangan et al., 2016 and Cameselle et al., 1986.

claim: Mycobacterium smegmatis has a cytoplasmic pH between pH 6.1 and 7.2.
source: While this charge selectivity makes sense in the uniquely high pH environment of S. elongatus PCC 7942, this compartment is also found in model bacteria that are known to have a lower cytoplasmic pH such as Mycobacterium smegmatis which has been measured to be between pH 6.1 and 7.2 (Rao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rao et al., 2001.

claim: Residues Arg 192 and Arg 304 confer the positive charge of the pore in S. elongatus PCC 7942 and are not well-conserved in other organisms.
source: Residues that conferred the positive charge of the pore in S. elongatus PCC 7942, Arg 192, and Arg 304, appear not to be well-conserved in other organisms.
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: The residues that appear most conserved at the fivefold pore are Gly 194 and Pro 196.
source: In contrast, the residues that appear most conserved are Gly 194 and Pro 196. These residues form the diameter of the inside of the pore.
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: The size of the pore is an important constraint for limiting the spectrum of substrates that can enter the compartment.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the size of the pore is also an important constraint for limiting the spectrum of substrates that can enter the compartment (Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Williams et al., 2018.

claim: The SrpI encapsulin fivefold pore is 3.7 Å in diameter at its most restrictive point.
source: The SrpI encapsulin fivefold pore is 3.7 Å in diameter at its most restrictive point (Figure 6C) as calculated by HOLE (Smart et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by pore analysis shown in Figure 6C and citation to Smart et al., 1996.

claim: Modeling of cysteine in the pore demonstrates it is likely small enough to enter the nanocompartment.
source: Furthermore, modeling of cysteine in the pore demonstrates it is likely small enough to enter the nanocompartment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by molecular modeling shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Symmetry expansion and focused classification of the holo-SrpI encapsulin revealed additional EM density at the interior surface of the shell that was localized to the three-fold symmetry axis.
source: However, symmetry expansion and focused classification of the holo-SrpI encapsulin, guided by the 225-NTD-sfGFP-SrpI dataset, revealed additional EM density at the interior surface of the shell that was localized to the three-fold symmetry axis (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Shell residues at the threefold axis neighboring the cargo EM density are highly conserved.
source: Of note, shell residues at the threefold axis neighboring the cargo EM density are highly conserved, which suggests that the interaction between the encapsulin cargo and shell may be conserved (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Residues F262 and Y273 are located near the suggested cargo density.
source: Namely, residues F262, and Y273 are located near the suggested cargo density.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the cargo density location.

claim: Unencapsulated CyD exhibited a kcat of 10 ± 4 s−1.
source: Unencapsulated CyD was active towards a cysteine substrate and exhibited a kcat of 10 ± 4 s−1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Encapsulated CyD was roughly sevenfold more active than unencapsulated CyD, with a kcat of 67 ± 5 s−1.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis that free cysteine could enter the SrpI encapsulin pore, we found that the encapsulated CyD was roughly sevenfold more active than unencapsulated CyD, with a kcat of 67 ± 5 s−1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The N-terminal domain had no effect on catalytic activity of CyD.
source: Importantly, the N-terminal domain had no effect on catalytic activity, and unloaded SrpI encapsulin did not exhibit any cysteine desulfurase activity.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Unloaded SrpI encapsulin did not exhibit any cysteine desulfurase activity.
source: Importantly, the N-terminal domain had no effect on catalytic activity, and unloaded SrpI encapsulin did not exhibit any cysteine desulfurase activity.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Rate enhancement of cargo enzymes by Family 1 encapsulins has been observed previously.
source: Rate enhancement of cargo enzymes by Family 1 encapsulins has been observed previously and is discussed below (Rahmanpour and Bugg, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahmanpour and Bugg, 2013.

claim: The Family 2 encapsulin structure shares the HK97 fold found in the Family 1 encapsulins.
source: We report here the first high-resolution structure for Family 2 encapsulins and find that it shares the HK97 fold found in the Family 1 encapsulins.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The electrostatic charge of the pore is likely reflective of the charge characteristics of the cargo substrate.
source: This contrast between pore charges suggests an overarching theme that may be shared among the encapsulins: the electrostatic charge of the pore is likely reflective of the charge characteristics of the cargo substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of Family 1 and Family 2 encapsulin structures and their respective substrates.

claim: The DyP-type peroxidase-containing encapsulin from Rhodococcus jostii exhibited an eightfold higher activity on a lignin substrate compared to the unencapsulated peroxidase.
source: One such example is the DyP-type peroxidase-containing encapsulin from Rhodococcus jostii, which was shown to exhibit an eightfold higher activity on a lignin substrate compared to the unencapsulated peroxidase (Rahmanpour and Bugg, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahmanpour and Bugg, 2013.

claim: The biochemical function of the FLP-containing encapsulin is impeded in the absence of shell protein, as it loses the ability to properly store and mineralize iron.
source: The biochemical function of the FLP-containing encapsulin is also impeded in the absence of shell protein, as it loses the ability to properly store and mineralize iron (He et al., 2016; McHugh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2016; McHugh et al., 2014.

claim: The protein SufE from E. coli has been shown to increase the activity of the cysteine desulfurase, SufS, 8- to 50-fold.
source: For example, the protein SufE from E. coli has been shown to increase the activity of the cysteine desulfurase, SufS, 8- to 50-fold (Loiseau et al., 2003; Outten et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Loiseau et al., 2003; Outten et al., 2003.

claim: SufE binding stimulates an allosteric change in SufS and enables faster regeneration of the SufS active site by the removal of persulfide from the SufS active site.
source: SufE binding stimulates an allosteric change in SufS and enables faster regeneration of the SufS active site by the removal of persulfide from the SufS active site, thereby allowing additional reaction cycles (Outten et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Outten et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2013.

claim: SrpI may be acting as an accessory protein for the activity of its cysteine desulfurase cargo analogous to what has been observed for SufE and SufS.
source: It is possible that SrpI may be acting as an accessory protein for the activity of its cysteine desulfurase cargo analogous to what has been observed for SufE and SufS.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to the SufE-SufS system.

claim: Cyanobacteria are assimilatory sulfate reducers.
source: Cyanobacteria are assimilatory sulfate reducers and thus, sulfate is sequentially reduced to sulfite and sulfide by the APS/PAPS pathway, which is then followed by the synthesis of L-cysteine via serine-O-acetyltransferase and cysteine synthase (Kopriva et al., 2008; Schmidt, 1990; Schmidt and Christen, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kopriva et al., 2008; Schmidt, 1990; Schmidt and Christen, 1978.

claim: Cyanobacteria that possess SrpI encapsulin genes are found in freshwater or brackish water, but not marine environments.
source: Furthermore, it is interesting to note that cyanobacteria that possess SrpI encapsulin genes are found in freshwater or brackish water, but not marine environments (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Sulfate is often a limiting nutrient in freshwater environments compared to marine habitats.
source: Sulfate is often a limiting nutrient in freshwater environments compared to marine habitats; therefore, the presence of SrpI exclusively in freshwater cyanobacteria suggests SrpI could play a role in sulfur starvation response (Giordano et al., 2005; Pilson, 2012; Tipping et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giordano et al., 2005; Pilson, 2012; Tipping et al., 1998.

claim: The presence of SrpI exclusively in freshwater cyanobacteria suggests SrpI could play a role in sulfur starvation response.
source: Sulfate is often a limiting nutrient in freshwater environments compared to marine habitats; therefore, the presence of SrpI exclusively in freshwater cyanobacteria suggests SrpI could play a role in sulfur starvation response (Giordano et al., 2005; Pilson, 2012; Tipping et al., 1998).
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of SrpI in freshwater cyanobacteria and the known sulfate limitation in freshwater environments.

claim: SrpI homologs from both M. leprae and M. avium are the most antigenic protein in human leprosy patients.
source: Previous work on a SrpI homolog from both M. leprae and M. avium has shown SrpI is the most antigenic protein in human leprosy patients (Winter et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winter et al., 1995.

claim: SrpI homologs have been proposed as a useful antigen for vaccine development in disease-causing Mycobacteria.
source: Because of its ability to elicit a proliferative T-cell response in leprosy patients, SrpI homologs have been proposed as a useful antigen for vaccine development in disease-causing Mycobacteria (Abdellrazeq et al., 2018; Abdellrazeq et al., 2020; Leite et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abdellrazeq et al., 2018; Abdellrazeq et al., 2020; Leite et al., 2015.

claim: Leite and colleagues enriched for a complex that was identified as MAP2121c and MAP2120c, the SrpI shell and cysteine desulfurase homologs respectively.
source: In their search for candidate antigens from M. avium subsp. paratuberculosis, Leite and colleagues enriched for a complex that was identified as MAP2121c and MAP2120c, the SrpI shell and cysteine desulfurase homologs respectively (Leite et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leite et al., 2015.

claim: An evolutionary relationship between the encapsulins and Caudovirales bacteriophages is clear given the shared HK97 fold of the capsid proteins.
source: An evolutionary relationship between the encapsulins and Caudovirales bacteriophages is clear given the shared HK97 fold of the capsid proteins.
evidence: This is supported by structural similarity and established knowledge in the field.

claim: It is possible that the HK97 fold derives from a cellular ancestor and was then recruited by a virus-like ancestor of Caudovirales phage.
source: It is possible that the HK97 fold derives from a cellular ancestor and was then recruited by a virus-like ancestor of Caudovirales phage (Krupovic and Koonin, 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Krupovic and Koonin, 2017.

claim: The HK97 fold was of viral origin and cellular hosts co-opted the compartments as proteinaceous organelles that enabled some fitness benefit.
source: Alternatively, the HK97 fold was of viral origin and cellular hosts co-opted the compartments as proteinaceous organelles that enabled some fitness benefit (Koonin and Krupovic, 2018; Krupovic and Koonin, 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Koonin and Krupovic, 2018; Krupovic and Koonin, 2017.
